note: Dense clonal stand of tall goldenrod in a field edge, with early yellow panicles just opening at upper left and the characteristic single unbranched stems densely clothed in narrow, alternate, sharply toothed lance-shaped leaves. Rubus canes with palmate/trifoliate toothed leaves fill the lower left foreground.

A row of small pure-white, shelving/kidney-shaped mushroom caps emerging from a crack in a decaying hardwood log, seen only from above. Gills, spore print, attachment and stipe (or lack of one) are not visible, so this cannot be placed even to genus — white shelf-formers on wood here could be oyster mushroom (Pleurotus), Crepidotus, or a young Pluteus/other agaric. A photo of the underside showing gill spacing and how they meet the wood would settle it.
Screened out: Blurry night photo of bare gravelly ground with sticks and pebbles; no plants or fungi present as a subject.

A single small salmon-orange capped mushroom on mossy, rocky forest floor, seen only from above and slightly out of focus. Gills, stem, flesh colour, spore print and any bruising reaction are not visible, so no genus can be assigned — a side view showing gill attachment and the stem base would be needed.

Center of frame shows a slender stem topped by a short, dense, bracted flower spike with a single open violet two-lipped flower — characteristic of Prunella vulgaris growing on leaf-littered forest floor. Distance and focus prevent checking the square stem, so confidence is medium.

Broad oval basal leaves with strong parallel ribs and prominent grooved petioles, plus slender dense cylindrical flower/seed spikes rising from the rosette — classic Plantago major. Fern fronds fill the background but are not identifiable to genus here.

Small seedling/sprout with opposite, broadly ovate, coarsely toothed leaves with strongly impressed pinnate veins and a dull blue-green surface — consistent with a Viburnum seedling. No flowers, fruit, or buds are visible, so species is not determinable; a mature shoot with fruit or the leaf-base/petiole detail (and whether stellate hairs are present beneath) would settle it. Worth rechecking, since the invasive Viburnum species and non-native honeysuckles also have opposite toothed leaves at this stage.

Rose shrub in a grassy coastal edge with ripening hips (still yellow-orange), persistent sepals, pinnately compound serrate leaflets and prickly stems — matches the existing Wild Rose entry. Species is not settled here; if leaflets are strongly wrinkled/rugose and hips are broad and squat, this could be the introduced Rosa rugosa, so check leaf texture and dense stem bristles.

A small conifer sapling (roughly knee-high, flat feathery branch sprays, slender nodding leader) on a bare, needle- and leaf-littered forest floor beside what appears to be a wooden post or sign base. The image is too soft to resolve individual needles — needle length, whether they are flat with two pale bands beneath (Tsuga/Abies) or four-sided and sharp (Picea), and the twig/bud detail are all unreadable, so even genus cannot be supported. A close photo of a twig underside and of the buds would settle it between eastern hemlock, balsam fir, and spruce.

Single non-flowering leafy stem on shaded forest floor: leaves alternate, narrowly lanceolate, entire to sparsely toothed, sessile and somewhat drooping, with a faint three-veined look — consistent with a vegetative goldenrod (Solidago, canadensis/altissima group). Without flower heads I cannot rule out a young aster (Symphyotrichum) or Eupatorium; the branched terminal panicle and rough triple-nerved leaves in bloom would settle it. Nothing here resembles a regulated invasive.

Single flowering stalk on a granite riprap shoreline: unbranched stem with a dense terminal spike of yellow flowers and thick, pale grey-green woolly leaves clasping and running down the stem — Verbascum thapsus. Rosette leaves visible at base.

A yellow-rayed composite in leaf litter along a woodland edge; the stem bears roughly opposite, sessile, lance-shaped leaves with three main veins from the base and a rough feel, and the heads have few broad yellow rays with a yellow disc — consistent with a woodland sunflower (Helianthus divaricatus). Flowers are blurred and the disc colour/phyllaries are not resolvable, so this is genus-level at best; a close shot of a head and of the leaf base would settle species.

Lacy, finely cut bipinnate-pinnatifid frond with tapering yellow-green pinnae and a slender straw-colored rachis on the forest floor, consistent with hay-scented fern; no sori or frond base visible, so a scaly-stiped Dryopteris cannot be fully excluded — crushing a pinna for the sweet hay smell would settle it.

A single dense, ashy-gray, repeatedly branched club-like fruiting body about 5 cm tall sitting on oak leaf litter; the fleshy, somewhat flattened and crested branch tips fit a gray coral fungus (Clavulina cf. cinerea) rather than a lichen. Without a close view of the flesh (brittle/fleshy vs. cartilaginous lichen podetia) or a spore print, a Cladonia reindeer-lichen clump cannot be fully excluded, so this is only a tentative genus call.
Basal rosette of broad, oval, strongly parallel-veined leaves on channelled petioles with leafless spikes rising from the centre — classic Plantago major.

Bright orange, wavy-lobed cup fungus sitting on mossy leaf litter (haircap moss, Polytrichum, surrounds it); the flaring, contorted cup shape and vivid orange colour fit Aleuria aurantia, but the underside/hymenium and any gill or vein pattern are not visible, so a young chanterelle cannot be fully excluded. Turning one over to check for a smooth spore surface versus false gills would settle it.

Central plant is a slender forest-floor herb with paired ovate, cordate-based, sparsely toothed leaves and a tiny terminal cluster of buds — best fit Circaea (enchanter's nightshade). IMPORTANT: the kidney-shaped, round-scalloped leaves at left and top of frame resemble first-year Alliaria petiolata (garlic mustard, a Maine regulated invasive); crushing one of those leaves to check for a distinct garlic/onion smell would settle it, and a flowering stem with 4-petaled white flowers would confirm.

Overlapping rosettes of thin, concentrically zoned brackets on a fallen birch/hardwood log, upper surfaces greened by algae — consistent with the weathered Trametes-type bracket entry already in the guide (likely T. versicolor). Pore surface is not visible, so species cannot be confirmed.

Several basal rosettes of broad, oval, strongly parallel-veined leaves with stout channelled petioles growing in compacted gravel along a building foundation — classic Plantago major. Taller dissected-leaved weeds behind it are too blurred to name.

Forest-floor litter dominated by fallen oak leaves with two shed acorns (shallow, scaly caps and short rounded nuts) beside a twig; the leaves are lobed and appear bristle-tipped, suggesting the red oak group, but they are too weathered to key to species. A hairy caterpillar (likely a spongy moth larva) is on the twig but is not a plant record.

Single firm, sessile, ochre-yellow ball sitting on leaf litter with a coarsely scaly/cracked surface typical of Scleroderma citrinum; interior not shown, so the diagnostic hard purple-black gleba could not be confirmed. Cutting one in half would settle it — earthballs are solid dark inside, true puffballs pure white.

Blurred forest-floor shot of leaf litter, bare twigs, and a tree trunk. The only green is a few out-of-focus small leaves on a twig at upper right, and a small yellow-orange patch at bottom that could be a jelly or crust fungus; neither shows enough detail (leaf arrangement, margin, fruiting structures) to name a genus.

Flat-topped clusters of white-rayed, yellow-centered heads on reddish-purple stems with narrow, entire, lance-shaped leaves and many rays per head — keys to flat-topped white aster (Doellingeria umbellata); a lance-leaved aster (Symphyotrichum lanceolatum) cannot be fully excluded without seeing the full inflorescence shape and phyllaries. A small bee is on one head.

Severely out-of-focus forest-floor shot between two tree trunks: green moss or low herbaceous growth, leaf litter, and blurred bark. No leaf shape, flower, or fruit detail is resolvable, so no taxon can be named. A sharp close-up of individual leaves or fruiting structures would be needed.

Dry open field with a stand of slender, reddish-stemmed plants bearing narrow opposite leaves and dense whorl-like clusters of small buds/flowers in the leaf axils — consistent with a mint-family plant (e.g. Lycopus, Mentha, or a hemp-nettle relative), but the image is too distant and soft to resolve flower shape, calyx teeth, leaf margins, or stem cross-section, so no genus can be given honestly. A close photo of a single flower whorl plus a leaf, and a note on whether the crushed stem is square and aromatic, would settle it. Large ovate leaves at upper left are Common Milkweed. Nothing here suggests a listed invasive, though a closer look would rule out Purple Loosestrife (which would have four-angled stems and a single terminal magenta spike).

Two small orange-capped mushrooms in hardwood leaf litter, photographed from above and out of focus, with a dark object (likely a boot or lens shadow) intruding at right. No view of the gills, stem base, or veil/ring, and no scale reference — orange caps this size could be Amanita (young), Hygrocybe, Cortinarius, or a small bolete. Cannot support even a genus; a cap turned over to show gills or pores plus the stem base would settle it.
Screened out: Photograph of an interpretive sign panel illustrating birds (seabirds in flight), not a photograph of plants, fungi, or vegetation.
Screened out: Image is completely out of focus — an unresolvable blur of pale brown and white shapes with no discernible plant, fungus, or landscape structure.

A colony of long-petioled, heart- to kidney-shaped basal leaves with shallowly crenate (scalloped) margins rising directly from the ground in leaf litter — consistent with a stemless violet (Viola sp.). No flowers or capsules are present, so species cannot be determined; a spring bloom would be needed to separate the blue, white, and yellow species.

Several rosettes of broad, oval, strongly parallel-veined leaves with thick petioles sprawling over compacted gravel along a building foundation — classic Plantago major. The taller erect plant behind it with narrow leaves and tiny white flowers may be smooth bedstraw or a chickweed relative but is too out of focus to key.

A single small tan, kidney-shaped bracket emerging from a fallen white-barked birch log on the forest floor; smooth suede-like upper surface, pale margin, and the exclusive birch host point to Fomitopsis betulina. The pore surface is not visible in this photo, which would confirm it — expect fine white pores and a rubbery-corky texture.

Roadside edge shot with several intergrown weeds: reddish stems with narrow lance-shaped leaves, a coarser toothed-leaf rosette plant in the foreground, and mixed grasses and broadleaf growth behind. No flowers, fruit, or clear close-up of any one plant, so nothing here can be taken past a guess — the red-stemmed plant could be a willowherb (Epilobium) or a knotweed-family plant but the leaf bases, stipules/ocrea, and any inflorescence are not visible. A close photo of a single stem showing the node (sheathing ocrea would point at Persicaria/Reynoutria) plus any flowers would settle it; note that a stout red-stemmed plant on a disturbed roadside should be checked against Japanese knotweed (Reynoutria japonica), which has hollow bamboo-like stems and broad truncate-based leaves — not what is shown, but worth a return visit.

Fallen acorns on bare trail soil — nuts with shallow, scaly, saucer-shaped caps still attached, which is enough to place them in Quercus but not to species; no leaves, twigs or bark are in frame to separate red-group from white-group oak.

Several rosettes of broad, oval, strongly ribbed leaves with the blade tapering into a channelled petiole, growing in compacted gravel along a building foundation — classic Plantago major. The upright plant behind it, with whorls of narrow leaves and tiny white flowers, is smooth bedstraw (Galium mollugo).

Dense stand of goldenrod in early bloom — lanceolate, sharply toothed, three-nerved leaves on unbranched stems with a plume-like panicle of small yellow heads, consistent with the Solidago canadensis group already catalogued.

Alternate, ovate, coarsely round-toothed leaves with a pale bluish-green cast and a swollen green ovoid seed capsule at a leaf axil, on a translucent succulent stem — consistent with Impatiens capensis. No open flower visible, so species rests on the capsule and foliage.

Dense colony of lacy, yellow-green, twice-cut fronds with broadly triangular blades tapering to a narrow tip and thin straw-colored stipes — consistent with hay-scented fern. Frond bases and undersides are not shown, so the ID rests on blade cut and colony habit; crushing a pinna for the sweet hay smell would confirm.

Distant, low-resolution shot of a single stout unbranched flowering stalk on a cobble/ledge shoreline. No clear view of leaf shape, arrangement, stem surface, or open flowers, so it cannot be placed even to genus — the dense yellow-green terminal spike is consistent with a shoreline goldenrod (Solidago, possibly S. sempervirens) in bud but equally with a young mullein (Verbascum thapsus) spike; a close photo of the basal leaves (fleshy and smooth vs. thick and woolly) and of the stalk would settle it. Scattered small yellow composite flowers in the surrounding turf are also too small in frame to name.

Slender erect stem with narrow, nearly sessile, opposite-to-alternate lance-shaped leaves and small four-petaled white-pink flowers with a long inferior ovary below each bloom — consistent with Epilobium (likely E. ciliatum) growing in gravel along a building foundation. Broadleaf plantain rosettes at the base.

Sprawling herbaceous patch with succulent branching stems, ovate coarsely toothed leaves and small orange spurred flowers dangling on thread-like pedicels — consistent with Impatiens capensis; a few orange blooms are visible upper center and left. Flower detail is blurry, so species-level confirmation of spur shape is not possible here.

A single brown-capped mushroom photographed from directly above in gravelly grass; the cap surface is dry and slightly lobed, but no view of the stipe, ring, or the underside (pores vs. gills) is available, and no cross-section or spore information. Without the hymenium it cannot be placed even to genus — flip it and photograph the underside and base to key it.

Young hoof-like tan bracket emerging laterally from a fallen white birch log — substrate (birch) plus the smooth, pale buff, kidney-shaped cap with an inrolled thin margin points to Fomitopsis betulina. The pore surface is not visible in this shot; checking for a fine white pore layer with a distinct sterile rolled edge would confirm it.

Dense low leafy growth of ovate simple leaves at the base of a mature tree, with grass in the foreground; no flowers, fruit, clear leaf arrangement, or twig detail is resolvable at this focus, so no genus can be supported. Worth rechecking on the ground: sprawling ovate-leaved shrubby growth like this at a tree base can be invasive bush honeysuckle (Lonicera morrowii/tatarica) — hollow pith in a cut twig, opposite leaves, and paired red berries would settle it.

Young multi-stemmed shrub with soft, entire (untoothed) oval leaves that appear to be borne in opposite pairs, pale green and slightly hairy — consistent with an invasive bush honeysuckle (Lonicera morrowii/tatarica) sapling, which is why I am flagging it. This is low confidence: no flowers or fruit are present and the opposite arrangement is not fully resolved in the photo. To settle it, snap a pencil-thick stem and look for a hollow brown pith (bush honeysuckle) versus solid white pith (native Diervilla, Viburnum, or Amelanchier); also confirm strictly opposite leaves. Upper-left of frame shows a toothed compound leaf that is a different plant (probable Rubus).
Dense terminal squarish flower spike with violet two-lipped flowers above bracts, opposite oval leaves on a low square stem — matches self-heal already in the guide.

A single fern frond photographed from above against leaf litter (a wooden post and a boot toe are also in frame). The blade is broadly triangular to lance-shaped, yellow-green, pinnate-pinnatifid with a pale rachis, which fits several genera — Dennstaedtia punctilobula and Thelypteris/Parathelypteris are both plausible — but the underside (sori/indusia), the stipe base and scales, and the frond base pinnae are not visible, and no hay-scent could be assessed. Not identifiable past 'a fern' from this image; a shot of the underside with sori plus the stipe base would settle it.

Colony of basal, hoof- to heart-shaped leaves with shallowly angular-toothed margins and palmate veining radiating from the notch, arising directly from the ground on stout petioles with no visible stem leaves — consistent with Coltsfoot as already catalogued. Turning a leaf to check for a white-woolly underside would confirm it.

A single small orange-brown mushroom cap seen only from above, out of focus, sitting on a mossy rock with gravelly soil. No view of the stem, gills or pores, no scale, and no flesh or spore detail — not enough for even a genus. A side view showing the underside and stem base would be needed.

A single lacy, broadly triangular, twice-to-thrice-cut frond with a pale yellow-green rachis and finely toothed, hairy-looking segments — consistent with hay-scented fern. Underside sori and the stipe base are not visible, so lady fern (Athyrium filix-femina, which has crescent/J-shaped sori and a grooved, scaly stipe) cannot be fully excluded; crushing a pinna and smelling for cut hay would settle it.

Slender erect stem with narrow, nearly opposite lance-shaped leaves and tiny notched pink-white four-petalled flowers in the upper axils — consistent with the Epilobium (willowherb) entry, most likely E. ciliatum, growing in gravel along a building foundation. Broadleaf plantain rosettes occupy the foreground.
Screened out: Photograph's subject is an interpretive display sign/signboard with printed text and illustration, not vegetation; surrounding plants are incidental and not identifiable.

Blurred ground-level shot of grass, mosses and leaf litter with a small bright orange-red mushroom cap partly hidden at center. The image is out of focus and the cap underside, gills, stem and spore surface are not visible, so even a genus (e.g. Hygrocybe vs. Amanita vs. Russula) cannot be supported; a sharp side view showing gills and stem base would settle it.

Basal rosette of heart-shaped, crenate-margined leaves on long petioles arising directly from the ground in leaf litter — consistent with a stemless blue violet (Viola sp.). No flowers present, so species cannot be determined; genus is the limit here.

Center of frame shows an erect square-stemmed herb with opposite toothed leaves and whorled clusters of small pale pink-white two-lipped flowers set in conspicuously bristly/spiny calyces — the key hemp-nettle combination. Broad ribbed rosette leaves at lower right are broadleaf plantain; a deeply dissected leaf at upper left belongs to a separate unidentified plant.

Stout unbranched stems with opposite, broad oblong leaves having a pale prominent midrib and finely downy undersides, growing along a disturbed roadside edge — consistent with Asclepias syriaca already in the guide.

Screened out: The subject of the photo is an animal (a small brown mammal, likely a woodchuck or porcupine) on a log, not vegetation; the surrounding foliage is only incidental background and too blurred to identify.

Single small yellow 5-petaled flower with glossy petals on a slender stem, with deeply 3-lobed/divided stem leaves — consistent with a Ranunculus (buttercup), so filed under the existing buttercup entry, though the small flower and thin stem suggest it may be a different species (e.g. R. abortivus/recurvatus group) rather than R. acris. Sepal position and achene head, not visible here, would settle the species. An acorn cap on the litter indicates oak overhead but the tree itself is not identifiable from this frame.

Blurry shot of a slender erect stem in a woodland edge/roadside opening bearing a short terminal spike with one pale violet two-lipped flower over green bracts, with widely spaced opposite lance-shaped leaves below — consistent with a lax, shaded form of self-heal (Prunella vulgaris). To confirm, check for a square stem in cross-section and the dense bracted head; if the stem is round and the flowers are in a slim one-sided raceme, reconsider a lobelia or Veronica instead.

Small whitish-cream coral fungi with repeatedly branched, blunt/crown-tipped tips arising from mossy leaf litter — consistent with a crown-tipped or crested coral (Artomyces/Clavulina/Ramaria group); tip shape and flesh texture are not resolved enough for species, so genus is given tentatively.

Scattered lacy, broadly triangular, yellow-green fronds arising singly from a creeping rhizome in dry oak leaf litter — the growth habit and finely cut, tapering blade fit hay-scented fern; crushing a pinna for the cut-hay smell would confirm. No fertile fronds or stipe close-up visible, so species remains probable rather than certain.

Forest-floor leaf litter (oak leaves, an acorn cap, a fallen log) with one very small yellow five-petalled flower on a thin stem near the centre. The flower is too small and blurred to resolve petal shape, sepals, or basal leaves, and no clear foliage can be tied to it — it could be a Ranunculus, Potentilla, or a small yellow composite. Close-ups of the flower face and the leaves at its base would settle it.

Blurred close-up of a decaying tree trunk with discolored, rotting bark; no leaves, buds, twigs or fruiting bodies are resolvable, so neither the tree nor any fungus present can be named. A sharp image showing leaves, intact bark texture, or a clear fruiting body would be needed.

Erect shrub with terminal pyramidal panicles of small white-pinkish 5-petaled flowers and alternate, narrowly elliptic, sharply toothed leaves on reddish-brown stems — consistent with Spiraea alba var. latifolia (meadowsweet). Goldenrod is flowering around it. Species-level separation from S. tomentosa was made on the white (not deep pink) flowers and lack of woolly leaf undersides visible here.

A single waxy, translucent-white stem with a nodding bell-shaped flower and scale-like bracts rising from leaf litter beside a fern — no green tissue at all, which is diagnostic for Monotropa uniflora. The lacy fern frond at left and scattered acorns are incidental.

A single dark, cracked, charcoal-like mass erupting from a smooth gray trunk in mixed woods — the classic look of a chaga sterile conk. I could not confirm the host is a birch from this distance (bark shows no obvious peeling or lenticel bands), and an ordinary bark burl or canker callus would look similar from afar; splitting it to reveal bright rusty-orange interior tissue would settle it.
Screened out: Photograph shows a laminated interpretive sign/panel close-up, not a plant, fungus, or vegetated landscape suitable for survey; background foliage is out of focus and indistinct.

Yellow five-petaled flowers with numerous prominent stamens, opposite small leaves, and reddish-brown ripening seed capsules on a branched, bushy stem in grassy field habitat — matches common St. John's Wort already in the guide.

Compound leaves in threes and fives with sharply toothed, wrinkled leaflets, whitish undersides and a reddish arching cane — a Rubus (raspberry/blackberry) shoot among grasses. No flowers or fruit visible to fix the species.

Cluster of yellow-green, finely cut, triangular-tapering fronds arching from the ground in dry oak leaf litter — consistent with hay-scented fern; the frond outline broadest near the base and narrowing to a long tip, with lacy twice-to-thrice cut pinnae, is what I keyed on. Crushing a pinna to check for the cut-hay smell (and feeling the fine hairs on the stipe/rachis) would confirm it against a young lady fern or spinulose wood fern.

Basal rosettes of large heart-shaped (cordate), coarsely toothed leaves on long petioles rising from dry conifer/hardwood litter — consistent with big-leaved aster (Eurybia macrophylla), which commonly forms non-flowering leafy colonies on shaded forest floor. No flowering stem is present, so the ID rests on leaf shape, the deep basal sinus and the dry woodland habitat; coltsfoot was considered but that species has white-woolly leaf undersides and prefers wet disturbed ground.

Opposite, coarsely toothed, hairy ovate leaves with small pale pinkish-purple two-lipped flowers in axillary whorls at the upper nodes — consistent with the hemp-nettle already catalogued. Image is soft, so the bristly swollen stem nodes and spine-tipped calyx teeth could not be confirmed.

Weathered, grayish shelf/bracket fungus emerging from a wound on a living hardwood trunk. Only the dark, algae-stained upper surface is visible — the pore surface, flesh color, thickness and any zonation are hidden, so even a genus call (Trametes, Bjerkandera, Fomes, Ganoderma remnant) is not supportable. A view of the underside pores and a section through the flesh would settle it.

Pinnately compound leaves ending in branched tendrils, scrambling over surrounding vegetation, with small pale-purple pea flowers visible — matches the existing Vicia sp. entry. Rubus canes are visible around it.

Dense stand of erect, reddish, apparently square stems with narrow sessile opposite leaves and slender terminal/upper-axillary spikes of small pinkish flowers — consistent with purple loosestrife, but the flowers are too small/washed out in this frame to confirm. Flagging as a possible regulated invasive: check for a distinctly 4-angled (square) stem, opposite or whorled sessile leaves with heart-shaped bases, and 5–6 crinkled magenta petals; if the stem is round and the leaves alternate with a 4-parted pink flower it is a willowherb (Epilobium) instead. Common milkweed leaves occupy the upper left of the frame.

Erect branching herb against a building foundation with narrow, opposite, toothed lance-shaped leaves and small pale pink four-petalled flowers borne on long slender inferior ovaries — the classic willowherb (Epilobium, likely E. ciliatum) look. Species-level ID would need a closer view of the stigma (club-shaped vs 4-lobed) and stem hairs.

A small cluster of waxy, chlorophyll-free white stems with nodding terminal flowers emerging from hardwood leaf litter — the classic look of Indian Pipe. The surrounding glossy ovate parallel-veined green leaves are a separate plant (likely Maianthemum canadense, Canada mayflower), not part of it; the white plant is too small in frame to confirm to species with certainty, but Monotropa uniflora is the only common single-flowered white one here.

A tall grass sward in an open field, photographed at ground level with the flowering heads out of focus and backlit. The narrow, spike-like panicles and wide flat blades are consistent with reed canary grass (Phalaris arundinacea) or a bluejoint/Calamagrostis, but no sharp view of a single inflorescence, ligule, or spikelet is available, so no genus can be assigned honestly. A close, in-focus shot of one seed head plus the leaf collar/ligule would settle it — worth re-checking, since a reed canary grass takeover of a wet field is a management concern.

A single unopened, tan, finely warted/dotted puffball-type fruitbody sitting on mossy soil beside a granite boulder, photographed only from above. Without a cut section (interior white and firm vs. purple-black and marbled) or a view of the base/stalk, this could be either a true puffball (Lycoperdon) or a toxic earthball (Scleroderma), so no genus can be given honestly. Surface here looks more scurfy-warted than spiny, which leans earthball, but that needs confirming.
Opposite, broad oval leaves with stout pale midrib on an unbranched stem, topped by a single young green follicle (seed pod) — Common Milkweed. Matches the existing catalogue entry.

Heavily motion-blurred shot of understory vegetation and a fallen limb; no leaf detail, flowers, or fruit are resolvable, and a possible animal shape near the branch cannot be made out either. Nothing in the frame supports identification to genus.

Habitat/structure shot of a large multi-stemmed hardwood rising from a rocky forest floor, photographed from below. The foliage is backlit and too distant to read leaf arrangement, margin, or venation clearly, and there is no fruit, flower, or close bark detail — the crown suggests a maple-like palmately lobed leaf but that cannot be confirmed from this image. A close photo of a single leaf (upper and lower surface) plus a bark close-up would settle the genus.

A single erect leafy stem with a reddish, faintly speckled main stem and large broadly ovate, abruptly pointed leaves with prominent pinnate veins — consistent with young/regrowth Japanese knotweed (Reynoutria japonica), which is on Maine's Do Not Sell list. Flagging at low confidence: no flowers, no clear view of the node sheath (ocrea) or leaf-base shape, and the leaf arrangement in this photo is ambiguous (knotweed is strictly alternate with hollow, jointed, bamboo-like stems and a truncate/squared leaf base). Check those three features on site to settle it — if leaves are truly opposite with arching veins, it is a Cornus shrub instead.

Erect ruderal herb at a building foundation with narrow, toothed, mostly opposite lance-shaped leaves, tiny notched pale pink-white flowers, and slender elongate capsules along the upper stem — consistent with Epilobium (likely E. ciliatum). Broadleaf plantain rosettes and a Rubus cane are in the foreground.

A dense basal clump of heart-shaped (cordate), crenate-toothed leaves on long petioles arising from a single crown on the forest floor — consistent with a stemless blue violet (Viola sp.). No flowers or capsules are present, so species cannot be settled; flower colour and whether petals/spur are hairy would separate V. sororia from V. labradorica and others.

Screened out: The subject of this photograph is an animal (a small land snail) resting on a leaf; the vegetation is only background context and no diagnostic plant features (flowers, fruit, stem, leaf arrangement) are shown.

Wide habitat shot of a late-summer old-field/meadow edge dominated by plume-flowered yellow goldenrod (Solidago), with flat-topped white composites (likely flat-topped white aster or boneset) mixed in and a young hardwood edge behind. Identified to genus only — no close view of leaves or stems, so species-level goldenrod ID is not supportable from this frame; nothing here suggests a watchlist invasive, though a closer look at any tall clumped stems with hollow, jointed canes would be needed to rule out Japanese knotweed in a field like this.

Habitat/structure shot: a large hardwood snag with a heart-rot cavity and a broken limb, in an open mixed-hardwood stand. No leaves are attached to the dead trunk and the bark is too weathered to key — no foliage, twig, or bud detail to separate maple, ash, or oak, so I can only record it as an unidentified hardwood snag. Background canopy foliage is small and glossy (possibly beech/birch) but not resolvable at this distance.

Dense mat of pleurocarpous and acrocarpous mosses with pale blue-green lichen (likely a Cladonia squamule crust or Hypogymnia-type foliose lichen) covering the base and buttress of a tree trunk. No capsules, leaf detail, or apothecia are visible at this resolution, so the mosses can only be logged as a mixed bryophyte community rather than identified to genus. [Catalogue entry "Mixed Moss and Lichen Mat (tree base)" removed: "mixed" in the name — a description of the photo, not a taxon. This photo remains unidentified.]

Close-up of a mossy tree trunk/log with pale grey-green squamulose basal scales and several stalked, flaring trumpet- or goblet-shaped podetia — classic Cladonia (pixie cup / trumpet lichen). Species-level ID would need cup margin detail (proliferating vs. entire) and chemical spot tests, so left at genus.

Pale grey-green pixie-cup lichens (Cladonia sp., trumpet/goblet-shaped podetia rising from a squamulose basal thallus) growing among moss on a rotting log or tree base. Species-level ID would require chemical spot tests and a close look at whether the cup surface is granular-soredate or corticate-squamulose, so I have kept it at genus.

Forest floor leaf litter (oak and maple leaves) with a dark, blackened, decaying mushroom cap and a small tan button-shaped fungus to its left. Neither shows gills, pores, stipe, or spore print, so no identification beyond 'a decayed agaric-type fungus' is possible from this angle.

Backlit canopy/habitat shot looking up through a mixed deciduous crown; some leaves appear palmately lobed (maple-like, possibly Acer rubrum or A. pensylvanicum) but every leaf is silhouetted against sky with no bark, twig, or fruit detail. Not identifiable beyond 'broadleaf forest canopy' — a photo of a low branch showing leaf arrangement (opposite vs alternate) and lobe shape would settle it.

Habitat shot of an eroded trail with exposed tree roots, compacted soil, scattered grass tufts and a mat of green pleurocarpous moss over the roots. No flowering structures, leaves or sporophytes are resolvable, so nothing can be named below the level of 'moss' — a close-up of leaf shape and capsules would be needed for genus. [Catalogue entry "Trailside Moss (unidentified)" removed: 'Bryophyta sp.' is a rank above genus, not an organism. This photo remains unidentified.]

Bark-only photo of a mature trunk (~40+ cm diameter) with long, narrow vertical plates that curl loose at the edges, giving a shaggy look; no leaves, twigs, buds, or fruit are visible on the subject tree, so this cannot be taken past 'unidentified hardwood.' The shagginess fits an old red maple (Acer rubrum) or a large aspen/poplar, and superficially resembles shagbark hickory (Carya ovata); a look up at the canopy leaves or a fallen leaf at the base would settle it. [Catalogue entry "Unidentified mature hardwood (bark only)" removed: "unidentified" in the name — a description of the photo, not a taxon. This photo remains unidentified.]

Mixed-forest interior shot taken from below: a young conifer with self-pruned, persistent dead lower branches occupies the foreground, with maple-leaved hardwoods and gray-barked trunks behind. No close view of needles, cones, buds or bark texture, so the conifer can only be called a spruce/fir/hemlock-type evergreen — a branchlet showing needle cross-section (four-sided and sharp = spruce, flat and blunt with white bands = fir or hemlock) would settle it. Nothing here suggests a regulated invasive.

Extreme close-up of a young, warty, downy follicle (seed pod) with a curved beak on a stout hairy stalk, backed by a large entire leaf with a pale midrib — consistent with Common Milkweed in mid-August. No flowers, full leaf arrangement, or sap visible, so species is inferred from pod texture and habit.

Two flat-topped white compound umbels with finely divided ferny foliage at the grassy edge of a goldenrod stand — classic wild carrot. Umbels are still flat/open rather than curled into a bird's nest; no purple central floret visible at this resolution.

This is a habitat/landscape shot of a second-growth mixed hardwood understory along an old dry-laid stone wall and rubble pile. The central tree has smooth-to-shallowly ridged gray bark with epicormic sprouts bearing ovate, pinnately veined, serrate leaves, and the shoot near the trunk looks possibly pinnately compound (ash-like), but no bud, twig, fruit, or clear leaf-arrangement detail is visible, so I cannot key it past 'unidentified hardwood'. Nothing here clearly reads as a watchlist invasive, though the leafy shrub at right could be a bush honeysuckle or glossy buckthorn — check for opposite leaves and hollow pith (honeysuckle) versus alternate leaves with 8+ parallel vein pairs and thornless twigs (buckthorn) to settle it.

This is a wide habitat shot of a disturbed, eroded gully with an exposed pipe or culvert at the woodland edge, not a photo of a single specimen. Several plants are present — narrow-leaved herbs at left that could be goldenrod (Solidago), a leafy rosette-like stem in the center foreground, brambles and young hardwood saplings — but none is shown close enough (no flowers, no leaf detail, no stem view) to key reliably. Worth a return visit: disturbed soil around culverts is exactly where Japanese knotweed, bush honeysuckle, and glossy buckthorn establish, and the coarse-leaved shrubby growth mid-frame cannot be ruled out from this distance; a close photo of leaf arrangement (alternate vs. opposite) and stem (hollow and jointed vs. solid) would settle it.

Photo appears inverted/rotated: leaf litter and stipe bases occupy the upper frame with a colony of lacy, finely divided fern fronds below. Only distant, out-of-focus blades are shown — no pinnule detail, rachis grooving, or sori are visible, so this cannot be taken past 'fern'. The overall lacy, twice-to-thrice-cut look and dense colonial habit is consistent with hay-scented fern (Dennstaedtia punctilobula) or lady fern (Athyrium filix-femina), but the photo does not settle it. [Catalogue entry "Fern (unidentified colony)" removed: 'Polypodiopsida sp.' is a rank above genus, not an organism. This photo remains unidentified.]

Habitat shot of a cobble/sand beach with a single isolated clump of coarse grass at the tide line; too distant to see ligules, spikelets or rhizomes. Salt-tolerant shoreline grass, most likely a cordgrass (Spartina/Sporobolus), but a photo of the inflorescence and leaf base is needed to confirm even the genus.

Tall thicket-forming shrub with alternate, oval, abruptly pointed leaves and many small red-ripening fruits borne in elongate clusters along the twigs — consistent with chokecherry (Prunus virginiana) in mid-August, when fruit is red before turning near-black. IMPORTANT: the glossy leaves with strongly parallel lateral veins in this shot also raise glossy buckthorn (Frangula alnus, a Maine regulated invasive); settle it in person by checking leaf margins (chokecherry finely and sharply toothed, buckthorn entire/untoothed) and fruit arrangement (chokecherry in a long drooping raceme from one stalk, buckthorn in small tight axillary clusters), plus the bitter-almond smell of scraped chokecherry twigs.

Dogwood shrub in fruit: opposite, entire, strongly veined leaves crowded toward branch tips, bright red pedicels/infructescence branches, and blue-black drupes — features pointing to Cornus alternifolia (alternate-leaved / pagoda dogwood); leaf arrangement along the lower stem would settle alternate vs. opposite, so recording it under the existing Cornus sp. entry.
